title: Best External SSDs UK
short: Portable SSDs compared by sustained write speed, connector type and durability, from everyday drives to Thunderbolt 5 speed champions.
intro: A drive's rated speed is only part of the story: many cheaper SSDs slow down dramatically once their fast cache fills up on a large transfer. This guide compares drives tested by Tom's Hardware, which measures sustained write performance with a 15-minute Iometer benchmark rather than just peak burst speeds.

products.name: Pro-G40 SSD
products.best_for: Buyers who want a reliable, consistently fast all-rounder
products.key_spec: 1TB/2TB, Thunderbolt 3 with USB fallback, up to 2,700 MBps reads, 5-year warranty
products.summary: Tom's Hardware's overall pick, with both Thunderbolt 3 and USB modes so it works across a wide range of devices. Write performance is exceptional and consistent, wrapped in a metal and rubberised casing that stays cool and protects against knocks, though it commands a premium price.

products.name: EX400U
products.best_for: Buyers with a USB4 laptop who want speed without Thunderbolt 5 pricing
products.summary: Tom's Hardware measured read speeds above 4,000 MBps and sustained writes holding between 1,600-1,700 MBps for a full 15 minutes without drastically slowing down. A magnetic back lets it snap onto compatible phones for video recording, though the metal top gets hot during long sustained writes.
cons: Metal top gets hot during lengthy writes
Exterior finish looks a little cheap

products.name: Disk Pro
products.best_for: Buyers who want a drive that doubles as a hub on the road
products.key_spec: 1TB/2TB/4TB, 10 Gbps USB, built-in USB/HDMI hub, magnetic back
products.summary: Tom's Hardware called this one of the most genuinely useful drives it's tested, thanks to a built-in USB and HDMI hub that's handy when travelling with a laptop that's short on ports. Sustained writes stayed above 900 MB/s for the full 30-minute test, aided by active cooling.
pros: Built-in USB/HDMI hub is genuinely useful
cons: Cramped USB-C port won't fit bulky cable connectors

products.name: Rugged SSD4
products.best_for: Creators who move projects between Windows and Mac machines
products.key_spec: 1TB/2TB/4TB, USB4, ~4,000 MBps on Windows, ~3,440 MBps on Mac, 3-year warranty with data recovery
products.summary: Tom's Hardware found this the fastest drive it's tested across both Windows and Mac, with around 4,000/3,700 MBps read/write on Windows 11 and still-fast 3,440/3,093 MBps on a current Mac. The 3-year warranty includes data recovery, at a high price.
pros: Very fast on both Windows and Mac
Warranty includes 3 years of data recovery

products.name: T7 Touch
products.best_for: Buyers who want fast, easy hardware-level security
products.key_spec: 500GB/1TB/2TB, USB 3.2 Gen 2, built-in fingerprint scanner, AES 256-bit encryption
products.summary: Blends solid USB 3.2 Gen 2 performance with a built-in fingerprint scanner Tom's Hardware calls the most convenient way to unlock a drive it's seen, in an elegant aluminium shell available in several colours. The write cache is relatively small, and rivals like G-Technology's ArmorLock use phone-based unlocking that may be more secure.
pros: Includes both USB-A and USB-C cables

products.name: Rugged SSD Pro5
products.best_for: Mac users with Thunderbolt 5 who want the fastest possible drive
products.key_spec: 2TB/4TB, Thunderbolt 5, up to 6,700 MBps reads, 5-year warranty with data recovery
products.summary: The fastest single-drive speeds Tom's Hardware has recorded on an external SSD, tested on a Thunderbolt 5-equipped Mac, backed by 5 years of Seagate's data recovery service. Compatibility on older hardware is complex, and in Windows 11 over Thunderbolt 4 it was slower than newer native USB4 drives.
pros: 5 years of included data recovery service
cons: Slower than USB4 rivals without a Thunderbolt 5 port
Not supported over Thunderbolt 3 or low-power USB ports in Windows

guide.q: Why does sustained write speed matter more than the advertised spec?
guide.a: Most external SSDs use a fast cache that absorbs the first chunk of a transfer at top speed, then drops to much slower 'native' speeds once that cache fills up. If you regularly move large files or full folders, a drive's sustained performance under a long transfer matters more than its peak burst number on the box.

guide.q: USB, USB4 or Thunderbolt: what's the difference?
guide.a: Standard USB (up to 20 Gbps on recent drives) covers most everyday needs. USB4 roughly doubles that to 40 Gbps and is increasingly common on newer laptops. Thunderbolt adds guaranteed bandwidth and, at Thunderbolt 5, even higher speeds, but needs a Thunderbolt-equipped port on both ends to deliver its full performance.

guide.q: Do I need an external SSD or would a hard drive do?
guide.a: An external HDD, like the WD My Passport, is cheaper per terabyte and fine for archival storage or backups you rarely access. An SSD is faster, more durable against knocks since it has no moving parts, and far better suited to running programs or games directly from the drive.

guide.q: Is a MagSafe-compatible drive worth it?
guide.a: If you record video on a compatible iPhone or Android phone, a magnetic drive like the Corsair EX400U or Sharge Disk Pro here lets you snap it directly to the back of your phone for fast, cable-free offloading. It's a nice-to-have rather than essential for general laptop or desktop use.
